newsitem.title: USA: Chicago Fed favors state tax incentives in Midwest.
newsitem.headline: Chicago Fed favors state tax incentives in Midwest.

text.p: - The Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago recommanded on Wednesday that U.S. Midwest states introduce tax incentives to attract new investments to the booming economic region.

"Midwestern state governments have avoided major tax increases and expensive new spending programs. Policy-makers can act now to reconsider their use of selective tax abatements and their general tax structures to ensure that growth is encouraged and not inhibited," the Chicago Fed said while releasing its year-long study of the Midwest economy.
The study, "The Midwest Economy: Looking back to the Future," studied the reasons for the Midwest's rebound from its "rust belt"-era manufacturing slump and made recommendations for further growth.
"Aligning business tax structures more closely with the costs of the services provided by government could boost economic development in the Midwest," the study also said.

Chicago Fed President Michael Moskow, presenting the study's findings with his research staff, said the key to the Midwest's economic resurgence stemmed from the region's "willingness to reinvent itself."
Moskow said the Midwest's ability to adapt to new challenges should remain a key asset for future growth.
"Contributing to the Midwest's economic revival has been the critical restructuring of its industrial base," the study stressed.
Beside tax incentives, the Chicago Fed presented two other main recommendations -- higher training and education, and increasing use of new technology.
"To maintain the productivity improvements that were so important to the region's turn-around, the skills of all workers must be continuously upgraded," the study said.
Moskow stressed the equal importance of education and continuous training that translates into higher wages for skills found "not always in formal education."
The study also pointed out the manufacturing-heavy Midwest must continue to absorb new technologies.
"The Midwest economy will continue to improve if these new technologies and manufacturing processes can be transferred to more companies, both large and small," the study said.
The study acknowledged a somewhat bleaker outlook for the development of the rural Midwest where "with fewer workers required, job opportunities are reduced."
The Chicago Fed also noted Midwestern uneven fortunes for Midwestern metropolitan areas, "leaving redevelopment problems for the core city."
A main challenge for the Midwest remained the need to be competitive on international markets, mainly in developing countries that absorb about 40 percent of U.S. exports despite a rising dollar.

"This suggests the renewed demand for Midwestern goods is not simply due to a price advantage resulting from changes in the value of the dollar but from productivity increases, more open trade and investment policies," the study found.
